claim: Conditional ablation of Prohibitin 1 (PHB1) in Schwann cells causes a severe and fast progressing demyelinating peripheral neuropathy in mice.
source: We recently showed that conditional ablation of the mitochondrial protein Prohibitin 1 (PHB1) in SCs causes a severe and fast progressing demyelinating peripheral neuropathy in mice, but the mechanism that causes failure of myelin maintenance remained unknown.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous work (Della-Flora Nunes et al., 2021) and is presented as an established finding.

claim: mTORC1 and c-Jun are continuously activated in Schwann cells lacking Phb1.
source: Here, we report that mTORC1 and c-Jun are continuously activated in the absence of Phb1, likely as part of the SC response to mitochondrial damage.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including western blots showing increased levels of c-Jun and mTORC1 targets (Figure 1C and D).

claim: mTORC1 and c-Jun pathways are involved in the demyelination process in Phb1-SCKO animals.
source: Moreover, we demonstrate that these pathways are involved in the demyelination process, and that inhibition of mTORC1 using rapamycin partially rescues the demyelinating pathology.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing association between these pathways and demyelination markers, and rescue experiments with rapamycin.

claim: Inhibition of mTORC1 using rapamycin partially rescues the demyelinating pathology in Phb1-SCKO mice.
source: Moreover, we demonstrate that these pathways are involved in the demyelination process, and that inhibition of mTORC1 using rapamycin partially rescues the demyelinating pathology.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing morphological and functional improvements in rapamycin-treated Phb1-SCKO mice (Figure 7).

claim: Schwann cells provide essential trophic and metabolic support to nearby axons.
source: Therefore, SCs are believed to provide essential trophic and metabolic support to nearby axons (Nave, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature (Nave, 2010).

claim: Schwann cells identify axons larger than 1 μm in diameter and wrap them in multiple layers of myelin.
source: In addition, SCs identify axons larger than 1 μm in diameter and wrap them in multiple layers of a specialized membrane extension known as myelin.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field about Schwann cell biology.

claim: The myelin sheath reduces the capacitance of the axonal membrane.
source: The myelin sheath reduces the capacitance of the axonal membrane, and its discontinuous structure enables 'saltatory conduction', whereby ionic exchanges are concentrated in small myelin-free regions called nodes of Ranvier.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of myelin.

claim: The discontinuous structure of myelin enables saltatory conduction.
source: The myelin sheath reduces the capacitance of the axonal membrane, and its discontinuous structure enables 'saltatory conduction', whereby ionic exchanges are concentrated in small myelin-free regions called nodes of Ranvier.
evidence: This is established knowledge about myelin function.

claim: Preserved myelin ultrastructure was found in a 5000-year-old ice man.
source: Myelin is intuitively perceived as a stable structure, which can be exemplified by the remarkable discovery of preserved myelin ultrastructure in a 5000-year-old ice man (Hess et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Hess et al., 1998).

claim: Many myelin proteins and lipids show half-lives of months in brain.
source: This notion of stability was initially confirmed by studies investigating the turnover of myelin components in brain, with many myelin proteins and lipids showing half-lives of months (Smith and Eng, 1965; Fischer and Morell, 1974).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Smith and Eng, 1965; Fischer and Morell, 1974).

claim: Some myelin components have much faster turnover rates than others.
source: Nevertheless, even early studies were quick to point out that some of the myelin components had much faster turnover rates (Singh and Jungalwala, 1979; Sabri et al., 1974; Hayes and Jungalwala, 1976), suggesting that portions of the myelin (especially its non-compact regions) could be more dynamic.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Singh and Jungalwala, 1979; Sabri et al., 1974; Hayes and Jungalwala, 1976).

claim: Maintenance of myelin structure requires sustained expression of transcription factors EGR2 and SOX10 in Schwann cells.
source: Furthermore, we now know that maintenance of the myelin structure is not passive, requiring sustained expression of the transcription factors EGR2 (also known as Krox20) (Decker et al., 2006) and SOX10 (Bremer et al., 2011) in SCs, as well as continuous synthesis of myelin proteins (Meschkat et al., 2020) and lipids (Zhou et al., 2020) in brain.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Decker et al., 2006; Bremer et al., 2011).

claim: Myelin maintenance requires continuous synthesis of myelin proteins and lipids in brain.
source: Furthermore, we now know that maintenance of the myelin structure is not passive, requiring sustained expression of the transcription factors EGR2 (also known as Krox20) (Decker et al., 2006) and SOX10 (Bremer et al., 2011) in SCs, as well as continuous synthesis of myelin proteins (Meschkat et al., 2020) and lipids (Zhou et al., 2020) in brain.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Meschkat et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2020).

claim: Ablation of prohibitin 1 in Schwann cells greatly impairs myelin maintenance in the PNS.
source: We reported that ablation of the primarily mitochondrial protein prohibitin 1 (Phb1) in SCs greatly impairs myelin maintenance in the PNS (Della-Flora Nunes et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous work (Della-Flora Nunes et al., 2021).

claim: SC-specific deletion of Tfam leads to peripheral neuropathy phenotypes in mice.
source: In addition, SC-specific deletion of the mitochondrial transcription factor Tfam (Viader et al., 2011), the respiratory chain component Cox10 (Fünfschilling et al., 2012), the metabolic regulator Lkb1 (Beirowski et al., 2014; Pooya et al., 2014; Shen et al., 2014), the nicotinamide mononucleotide synthetizing enzyme Nampt (Sasaki et al., 2018), or the nutrient-sensing O-linked N-acetylglucosamine transferase Ogt (Kim et al., 2016), all lead to peripheral neuropathy phenotypes in mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Viader et al., 2011).

claim: SC-specific deletion of Cox10 leads to peripheral neuropathy phenotypes in mice.
source: In addition, SC-specific deletion of the mitochondrial transcription factor Tfam (Viader et al., 2011), the respiratory chain component Cox10 (Fünfschilling et al., 2012), the metabolic regulator Lkb1 (Beirowski et al., 2014; Pooya et al., 2014; Shen et al., 2014), the nicotinamide mononucleotide synthetizing enzyme Nampt (Sasaki et al., 2018), or the nutrient-sensing O-linked N-acetylglucosamine transferase Ogt (Kim et al., 2016), all lead to peripheral neuropathy phenotypes in mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Fünfschilling et al., 2012).

claim: SC-specific deletion of Lkb1 leads to peripheral neuropathy phenotypes in mice.
source: In addition, SC-specific deletion of the mitochondrial transcription factor Tfam (Viader et al., 2011), the respiratory chain component Cox10 (Fünfschilling et al., 2012), the metabolic regulator Lkb1 (Beirowski et al., 2014; Pooya et al., 2014; Shen et al., 2014), the nicotinamide mononucleotide synthetizing enzyme Nampt (Sasaki et al., 2018), or the nutrient-sensing O-linked N-acetylglucosamine transferase Ogt (Kim et al., 2016), all lead to peripheral neuropathy phenotypes in mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Beirowski et al., 2014; Pooya et al., 2014; Shen et al., 2014).

claim: SC-specific deletion of Nampt leads to peripheral neuropathy phenotypes in mice.
source: In addition, SC-specific deletion of the mitochondrial transcription factor Tfam (Viader et al., 2011), the respiratory chain component Cox10 (Fünfschilling et al., 2012), the metabolic regulator Lkb1 (Beirowski et al., 2014; Pooya et al., 2014; Shen et al., 2014), the nicotinamide mononucleotide synthetizing enzyme Nampt (Sasaki et al., 2018), or the nutrient-sensing O-linked N-acetylglucosamine transferase Ogt (Kim et al., 2016), all lead to peripheral neuropathy phenotypes in mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Sasaki et al., 2018).

claim: SC-specific deletion of Ogt leads to peripheral neuropathy phenotypes in mice.
source: In addition, SC-specific deletion of the mitochondrial transcription factor Tfam (Viader et al., 2011), the respiratory chain component Cox10 (Fünfschilling et al., 2012), the metabolic regulator Lkb1 (Beirowski et al., 2014; Pooya et al., 2014; Shen et al., 2014), the nicotinamide mononucleotide synthetizing enzyme Nampt (Sasaki et al., 2018), or the nutrient-sensing O-linked N-acetylglucosamine transferase Ogt (Kim et al., 2016), all lead to peripheral neuropathy phenotypes in mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Kim et al., 2016).

claim: mTOR is a serine/threonine kinase that regulates cellular growth and catabolism/anabolism rate according to the availability of nutrients and other cellular resources.
source: The mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) is a serine/threonine kinase that regulates cellular growth and catabolism/anabolism rate according to the availability of nutrients and other cellular resources (Saxton and Sabatini, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a review (Saxton and Sabatini, 2017).

claim: In Schwann cells, mTORC1 plays a dual role: high activity during development regulates SC proliferation and prevents premature differentiation, while low but continuous activity in myelinating SCs drives myelin sheath growth.
source: In SCs, mTORC1 plays a dual role: its high activity during development regulates SC proliferation and prevents premature differentiation, while its low but continuous activity in myelinating SCs drives myelin sheath growth (Beirowski et al., 2017; Figlia et al., 2017; Jiang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Beirowski et al., 2017; Figlia et al., 2017; Jiang et al., 2018).

claim: mTORC1 phosphorylates 4E-BP1 and S6K as substrates.
source: mTORC1 phosphorylates several substrates, among which are the extensively studied 4E-BP1 and ribosomal protein S6 kinase (S6K).
evidence: This is established knowledge about mTORC1 signaling.

claim: S6K phosphorylates the 40S ribosomal protein S6.
source: S6K, in turn phosphorylates many other proteins, the first identified being the 40S ribosomal protein S6.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mTORC1 signaling pathway.

claim: In Schwann cells, S6K mediates the developmental suppression of EGR2, preventing precocious SC differentiation.
source: In SCs, the specific downstream targets of mTORC1 have seldomly been explored, but S6K seems to mediate the developmental suppression of EGR2, preventing precocious SC differentiation (Figlia et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Figlia et al., 2017).

claim: mTORC1 is temporarily activated after nerve injury to induce expression of c-Jun.
source: mTORC1 is also temporarily activated after nerve injury to induce expression of c-Jun (an AP-1 transcription factor) (Norrmén et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Norrmén et al., 2018).

claim: c-Jun is the master transcription factor orchestrating the transdifferentiation of SCs to a repair phenotype.
source: c-Jun is the master transcription factor orchestrating the transdifferentiation of SCs to a repair phenotype that mounts a response favoring axon regrowth, tissue reinnervation and clearance of myelin debris (Jessen and Mirsky, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a review (Jessen and Mirsky, 2019).

claim: Transdifferentiation of myelinating SCs involves myelin removal followed by autophagic degradation (myelinophagy).
source: In the case of myelinating SCs, this transdifferentiation process involves myelin removal followed by its autophagic degradation (myelinophagy) (Gomez-Sanchez et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Gomez-Sanchez et al., 2015).

claim: Enforced Jun expression is sufficient to trigger demyelination.
source: This, associated to the fact that enforced Jun expression is sufficient to trigger demyelination (Fazal et al., 2017), raises the possibility that c-Jun and mTORC1 may play a role in the dismantling of myelin in the context of peripheral neuropathies.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Fazal et al., 2017).

claim: Phb1-SCKO mice show the first signs of myelin loss at postnatal day 20 (P20).
source: Mice lacking Phb1 in SCs (Phb1-SCKO) show the first signs of myelin loss at postnatal day 20 (P20), with demyelination peaking around P40-P60 and causing partial or complete hindlimb paralysis around P90 (Della-Flora Nunes et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous work (Della-Flora Nunes et al., 2021).

claim: Demyelination in Phb1-SCKO mice peaks around P40-P60.
source: Mice lacking Phb1 in SCs (Phb1-SCKO) show the first signs of myelin loss at postnatal day 20 (P20), with demyelination peaking around P40-P60 and causing partial or complete hindlimb paralysis around P90 (Della-Flora Nunes et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous work (Della-Flora Nunes et al., 2021).

claim: Phb1-SCKO mice develop partial or complete hindlimb paralysis around P90.
source: Mice lacking Phb1 in SCs (Phb1-SCKO) show the first signs of myelin loss at postnatal day 20 (P20), with demyelination peaking around P40-P60 and causing partial or complete hindlimb paralysis around P90 (Della-Flora Nunes et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous work (Della-Flora Nunes et al., 2021).

claim: Phb1-SCKO mice display axonal degeneration that follows a similar temporal progression to demyelination.
source: Concomitant with the demyelination, Phb1-SCKO mice also display axonal degeneration, which follows a similar temporal progression (Della-Flora Nunes et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous work (Della-Flora Nunes et al., 2021).

claim: There is progressive demyelination and axonal degeneration in the sciatic nerves of Phb1-SCKO animals.
source: There is progressive demyelination and axonal degeneration in the sciatic nerves of Phb1-SCKO animals.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1B from electron micrographs.

claim: SC apoptotic cell death is not greatly altered by deletion of Phb1 in vivo.
source: We also demonstrated that SC apoptotic cell death is not greatly altered by deletion of Phb1 in vivo, and that SC numbers remain normal in nerves of Phb1-SCKO, suggesting that a simple loss of viability cannot explain their pathology (Della-Flora Nunes et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous work (Della-Flora Nunes et al., 2021).

claim: SC numbers remain normal in nerves of Phb1-SCKO mice.
source: We also demonstrated that SC apoptotic cell death is not greatly altered by deletion of Phb1 in vivo, and that SC numbers remain normal in nerves of Phb1-SCKO, suggesting that a simple loss of viability cannot explain their pathology (Della-Flora Nunes et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous work (Della-Flora Nunes et al., 2021).

claim: Deletion of Phb1 leads to upregulation of c-Jun in sciatic nerves.
source: Representative western blot from sciatic nerve lysates reveal that deletion of Phb1 leads to upregulation of c-Jun and increased total and phosphorylated levels of the mTORC1 targets S6 and 4E-BP1.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1C and quantified in Figure 1D.

claim: Deletion of Phb1 leads to increased total and phosphorylated levels of the mTORC1 targets S6 and 4E-BP1.
source: Representative western blot from sciatic nerve lysates reveal that deletion of Phb1 leads to upregulation of c-Jun and increased total and phosphorylated levels of the mTORC1 targets S6 and 4E-BP1.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1C and quantified in Figure 1D.

claim: Phb1-SCKO animals only show minor changes in the ERK 1/2 pathway.
source: We had previously reported that phosphorylation of eIf2α is actually protective in Phb1-SCKO mice. In addition, Phb1-SCKO mice only show minor changes in the ERK 1/2 pathway, which are probably insufficient to initiate demyelination (Della-Flora Nunes et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous work (Della-Flora Nunes et al., 2021).

claim: Phb1-SCKO mice show only minor changes in the AKT pathway.
source: The same is true for the AKT pathway (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Phb1-SCKO animals show no differences in the phosphorylation levels of mTOR at Ser2448.
source: Nonetheless, we found no differences in the phosphorylation levels of mTOR at Ser2448 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the AKT/PI3K pathway is not involved in activating the mTORC1 pathway in Phb1-SCKO mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The AKT/PI3K pathway is not involved in activating the mTORC1 pathway in Phb1-SCKO mice.
source: Nonetheless, we found no differences in the phosphorylation levels of mTOR at Ser2448 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the AKT/PI3K pathway is not involved in activating the mTORC1 pathway in Phb1-SCKO mice.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the lack of changes in mTOR phosphorylation at Ser2448.

claim: Infiltrating macrophages do not seem to activate c-Jun and mTORC1 in sciatic nerves of Phb1-SCKO mice.
source: Although we cannot completely rule out the contribution of other nerve cells to the levels of c-Jun, 4E-BP1 and S6, infiltrating macrophages do not seem to activate c-Jun and mTORC1 in sciatic nerves of Phb1-SCKO mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 4), suggesting that these alterations may primarily occur in SCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The mitochondrial unfolded protein response (mtUPR) is believed to be partly regulated by binding of an AP-1 transcription factor (postulated to be c-Jun) to the promoter of CHOP and C/EBPβ.
source: The mitochondrial unfolded protein response (mtUPR) is believed to be partly regulated by binding of an AP-1 transcription factor (postulated to be c-Jun) to the promoter of CHOP and C/EBPβ (Horibe and Hoogenraad, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Horibe and Hoogenraad, 2007).

claim: mTORC1 was shown to be upstream of the integrated stress response (ISR) in muscle, regulating the progression of a mitochondrial myopathy.
source: On the other hand, mTORC1 was shown to be upstream of the integrated stress response (ISR) in muscle, regulating the progression of a mitochondrial myopathy (Khan et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Khan et al., 2017).

claim: Short-term treatment (24 h) with FCCP, oligomycin, or antimycin A resulted only in minor changes in c-Jun, mTORC1, ISR, and mitochondrial pathways in primary rat Schwann cells.
source: Short-term treatment (24 h) with these compounds resulted only in minor changes in these pathways (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Cells treated with FCCP for 24 hr presented with elevated levels of p-eIF2α and reduced ratio between the long and short isoforms of Opa1.
source: Cells treated with FCCP for 24 hr presented with elevated levels of p-eIF2α and reduced ratio between the long and short isoforms of Opa1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: The ISR can quickly be activated directly downstream of compromised mitochondria.
source: This is in line with previous reports showing that the ISR can quickly be activated directly downstream of compromised mitochondria (Viader et al., 2013; Mick et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Viader et al., 2013; Mick et al., 2020).

claim: A 7-day treatment of SCs with Oligomycin or Antimycin A triggered robust stimulation of the ISR.
source: On the other hand, a 7-day treatment of SCs with Oligomycin or Antimycin A triggered robust stimulation of the ISR (Figure 2A and B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A and B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: A 7-day treatment of SCs with Oligomycin or Antimycin A induced a potent activation of the mTORC1 pathway.
source: Furthermore, this lengthier treatment regimen also induced a potent activation of the mTORC1 pathway (Figure 2A and B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A and B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: c-Jun immunoreactivity was significantly associated with the presence of compromised mitochondria in Phb1-SCKO mice at P40.
source: Staining of individual myelinated fibers with c-Jun indicated that c-Jun immunoreactivity was significantly associated with the presence of compromised mitochondria (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: 78.81% of all SCs with damaged mitochondria showed strong c-Jun nuclear expression in Phb1-SCKO mice at P40.
source: Moreover, 78.81% of all SCs with damaged mitochondria showed strong c-Jun nuclear expression, while only 23.15% of SCs with reasonably well-preserved mitochondria stained positive for c-Jun (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Only 23.15% of SCs with reasonably well-preserved mitochondria stained positive for c-Jun in Phb1-SCKO mice at P40.
source: Moreover, 78.81% of all SCs with damaged mitochondria showed strong c-Jun nuclear expression, while only 23.15% of SCs with reasonably well-preserved mitochondria stained positive for c-Jun (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: No association was identified between mitochondrial loss and expression of p-S6 in Phb1-SCKO mice at P40.
source: In contrast, we did not identify any association between mitochondrial loss and expression of p-S6 (Figure 3D–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D–F.

claim: All evaluated fibers containing myelin ovoids showed intense nuclear c-Jun staining in Phb1-SCKO mice at P40.
source: In our analysis, all the evaluated fibers containing myelin ovoids showed intense nuclear c-Jun staining (Figure 4A–C), suggesting a strong association between c-Jun expression and demyelination.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A–C.

claim: There is a correlation between p-S6 and the presence of myelin ovoids in Phb1-SCKO mice at P40.
source: Similarly, we also identified a correlation between p-S6 and the presence of myelin ovoids (Figure 4D and E), and a greater proportion of the SCs containing myelin ovoids were also positive for p-S6, although this difference did not reach statistical significance (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4D and E.

claim: The mRNA expression of Gdnf, Shh, Cdh1, Mbp, and Mpz is altered in Phb1-SCKO mice in the expected direction for c-Jun activation.
source: We found that the mRNA expression of the majority of the genes evaluated is altered in Phb1-SCKO mice in the expected direction: upregulation of Gdnf and Shh; downregulation of Cdh1, Mbp and Mpz (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: No change in expression of Olig1 was identified in Phb1-SCKO mice.
source: We did not, however, identify any change in expression of Olig1.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Phb1-SCKO mice showed overexpression of Mixed lineage kinase domain-like (MLKL).
source: Phb1-SCKO mice also showed overexpression of Mixed lineage kinase domain-like (MLKL), a protein recently implicated in dismantling the myelin sheath after nerve injury (Ying et al., 2018; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and D.

claim: MLKL was recently implicated in dismantling the myelin sheath after nerve injury.
source: Phb1-SCKO mice also showed overexpression of Mixed lineage kinase domain-like (MLKL), a protein recently implicated in dismantling the myelin sheath after nerve injury (Ying et al., 2018; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Ying et al., 2018).

claim: Deletion of Phb1 in SCs resulted in upregulation of the autophagic machinery.
source: Moreover, deletion of Phb1 in SCs also resulted in upregulation of the autophagic machinery, which is important for myelinophagy and is regulated by c-Jun after nerve injury (Gomez-Sanchez et al., 2015; Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: Autophagic machinery is important for myelinophagy and is regulated by c-Jun after nerve injury.
source: Moreover, deletion of Phb1 in SCs also resulted in upregulation of the autophagic machinery, which is important for myelinophagy and is regulated by c-Jun after nerve injury (Gomez-Sanchez et al., 2015; Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Gomez-Sanchez et al., 2015).

claim: Activation of the ISR frequently leads to alterations in the mTORC1 pathway.
source: Activation of the ISR frequently leads to alterations in the mTORC1 pathway (Ryoo and Vasudevan, 2017; Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Ryoo and Vasudevan, 2017; Zhang et al., 2019).

claim: Inhibition of the ISR using ISRIB did not significantly alter p-S6, c-Jun or Opa1 expression in Phb1-SCKO mice.
source: Inhibition of the ISR using a daily injection of 2.5 mg/kg ISRIB as previously reported (Della-Flora Nunes et al., 2021) did not significantly alter p-S6, c-Jun or Opa1 expression in Phb1-SCKO mice (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5.

claim: ISRIB treatment was sufficient to result in a small reduction in levels of p-4E-BP1 and 4E-BP1 in Phb1-SCKO mice.
source: Nonetheless, this treatment was sufficient to result in a small reduction in levels of p-4E-BP1 and 4E-BP1 (Figure 5B and C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5B and C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Presence of one or two Jun floxed alleles resulted in a significant and dose-dependent reduction in c-Jun protein levels in sciatic nerves at P40.
source: At P40, presence of one (Phb1-SCKO; JUN Het) or two Jun floxed alleles (Phb1; JUN SCKO) resulted in a significant and dose-dependent reduction in c-Jun protein levels in sciatic nerves (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Reduction in c-Jun led to a dose-dependent reduction in the number of demyelinated fibers and myelinophagy events in Phb1-SCKO mice.
source: As expected, this reduction in c-Jun also led to a dose-dependent reduction in the number of demyelinated fibers and myelinophagy events (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological data shown in Figure 6B and C.

claim: Deletion of Jun in Phb1-SCKO mice caused a dose-dependent reduction in the number of myelinated axons in tibial nerves.
source: Nevertheless, deletion of Jun in Phb1-SCKO mice also caused a dose-dependent reduction in the number of myelinated axons in tibial nerves (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological data shown in Figure 6B and C.

claim: Nerves of Phb1; JUN SCKO contained bundles with large non-myelinated axons and a visible division of the nerve in smaller fascicles (hyper-fasciculation).
source: In addition, nerves of Phb1; JUN SCKO contained bundles with large non-myelinated axons and a visible division of the nerve in smaller fascicles (hyper-fasciculation) (Figure 6B and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological data shown in Figure 6B and D.

claim: Ablation of Jun in SCs already lacking Phb1 may exacerbate the mild developmental defects previously observed in Phb1-SCKO mice.
source: These phenotypes suggest that ablation of Jun in SCs already lacking Phb1 may exacerbate the mild developmental defects that we previously observed in Phb1-SCKO mice (Della-Flora Nunes et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observed phenotypes and previous findings.

claim: Jun deletion is not sufficient to rescue the motor deficits of Phb1-SCKO mice in the rotarod.
source: As a consequence, Jun deletion is not sufficient to rescue the motor deficits of Phb1-SCKO mice in the rotarod (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Deletion of Jun has a dose-dependent effect on levels of p-4E-BP1 in Phb1-SCKO mice.
source: Deletion of Jun in Phb1-SCKO mice had a dose-dependent effect on levels of p-4E-BP1 and also reduced p-S6 when both Jun alleles were deleted, suggesting that c-Jun may partially modulate mTORC1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Deletion of both Jun alleles reduced p-S6 in Phb1-SCKO mice.
source: Deletion of Jun in Phb1-SCKO mice had a dose-dependent effect on levels of p-4E-BP1 and also reduced p-S6 when both Jun alleles were deleted, suggesting that c-Jun may partially modulate mTORC1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: c-Jun may partially modulate mTORC1 in Phb1-SCKO mice.
source: Deletion of Jun in Phb1-SCKO mice had a dose-dependent effect on levels of p-4E-BP1 and also reduced p-S6 when both Jun alleles were deleted, suggesting that c-Jun may partially modulate mTORC1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observed effects of Jun deletion on mTORC1 targets.

claim: c-Jun does not seem to be important to regulate the ISR in Phb1-SCKO mice.
source: c-Jun, however, does not seem to be important to regulate the ISR, since p-eIF2α levels are unaltered in Phb1-SCKO mice upon Jun deletion (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data showing no change in p-eIF2α levels upon Jun deletion.

claim: Ablation of Jun is unable to alter the mRNA levels of ATF4 targets in Phb1-SCKO mice.
source: In agreement with this finding, ablation of Jun is also unable to alter the mRNA levels of ATF4 targets (Asns, Chac1, Pck2, and Ddit3, also known as Chop), which are upregulated downstream of p-eIF2α during ISR in Phb1-SCKO mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Rapamycin treatment was efficient and significantly reduced the levels of p-4E-BP1 and p-S6 in sciatic nerves of P40 Phb1-SCKO mice.

claim: The main beneficial effect of rapamycin on Phb1-SCKO mice is in preventing their demyelination.

claim: Treatment with rapamycin should reduce global translation levels.

evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about rapamycin's mechanism of action.
